author: Cecilia Nobre
summary: A short, sharp note on delayed error correction in language teaching that questions what the routine actually measures. Nobre reconstructs the familiar sequence, a learner's error written on the board after a speaking task, the class inspecting it, someone naming the fix, and points out that the task has silently changed between the utterance and the correction. The student who produced the error was operating under real-time processing pressure, attending to meaning rather than form. The student who fixes it on the board is editing a decontextualised sentence with unlimited time. She is careful not to dismiss the activity, conceding that it is useful, while denying that it is evidence the learner can avoid the same error while speaking. The closing claim is the one worth keeping: delayed correction flatters our sense of how controllable language is, compared with how it feels mid-story when the brain is already doing several other jobs.
points: Identifies a quiet task substitution in a standard correction routine, where real-time production is replaced by untimed editing.
Separates the usefulness of board-based correction from its value as evidence, which is the distinction most staffroom discussion skips.
Grounds the objection in processing load rather than in a claim that correction is harmful.
Argues the practice makes language look more controllable than it feels to a learner halfway through telling a story.
quotes: But the student who originally said it may have been communicating fluently, focusing on meaning, and not noticing the form at all.
5 minutes later, the sentence is sitting alone on the board under forensic lighting.
The learner is no longer producing language in real time. They’re editing a decontextualised sentence with unlimited processing time.
Evidence that they can avoid the same error while speaking? Not yet.
Delayed correction can make language look much more controllable than it feels when you’re halfway through telling a story and your brain has 6 other jobs.
